{{short description|Special function defined by an integral}}
{{distinguish|text=[[List of integrals of exponential functions|other integrals]] of [[exponential function]]s}}
{{use American English|date = January 2019}}
[[File:Plot of the exponential integral function E n(z) with n=2 in the complex plane from -2-2i to 2+2i with colors created with Mathematica 13.1 function ComplexPlot3D.svg|alt=Plot of the exponential integral function E_n(z) with n=2 for complex z|thumb|Plot of the exponential integral function {{math|''E''{{sub|2}}(''z'')}} for complex {{mvar|z}}]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''exponential integral''' {{tmath|\operatorname{Ei} }} is a [[special function]] on the [[complex plane]].
It is defined as one particular [[definite integral]] of the ratio between an [[exponential function]] and its [[argument of a function|argument]].

== Definitions ==
For real non-zero values of&nbsp;{{tmath|x}}, the exponential integral {{tmath|\operatorname{Ei}(x)}} is defined as
<math display="block"> \operatorname{Ei}(x) = -\int_{-x}^\infty \frac{e^{-t}}t\,dt = \int_{-\infty}^x \frac{e^t}t\,dt.</math>

The [[Risch algorithm]] shows that {{tmath|\operatorname{Ei} }} is not an [[elementary function]].  The definition above can be used for positive values of&nbsp;{{tmath|x}}, but the integral has to be understood in terms of the [[Cauchy principal value]] due to the singularity of the integrand at zero.

For complex values of the argument, the definition becomes ambiguous due to [[branch points]] at {{tmath|0}} and {{tmath|\infty}}.{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=228}} Instead of {{tmath|\operatorname{Ei} }}, the following notation is used,{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=228|loc=5.1.1}}
<math display="block">E_1(z) = \int_z^\infty \frac{e^{-t}}{t}\,  dt,\qquad|{\operatorname{Arg}}(z)|<\pi</math>
[[File:Plot of the exponential integral function Ei(z) in the complex plane from -2-2i to 2+2i with colors created with Mathematica 13.1 function ComplexPlot3D.svg|alt=Plot of the exponential integral function Ei(z) for complex z|thumb|Plot of the exponential integral function {{math|Ei(''z'')}} for complex {{mvar|z}}]]

For positive values of&nbsp;{{tmath|x}}, we have {{tmath|1= -E_1(x) = \operatorname{Ei}(-x) }}.

In general, a [[branch cut]] is taken on the negative real axis and {{tmath|E_1}} can be defined by [[analytic continuation]] elsewhere on the complex plane.

For positive values of the real part of {{tmath|z}}, this can be written{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=228|loc=5.1.4 with ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1}}
<math display="block">E_1(z) = \int_1^\infty \frac{e^{-tz}}{t}\, dt = \int_0^1 \frac{e^{-z/u}}{u}\, du ,\qquad \Re(z) \ge 0.</math>

The behaviour of {{tmath|E_1}} near the branch cut can be seen by the following relation:{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=228|loc=5.1.7}}
<math display="block">\lim_{\delta\to0+} E_1(-x \pm i\delta) = -\operatorname{Ei}(x) \mp i\pi,\qquad x>0.</math>

== Properties ==
Several properties of the exponential integral below, in certain cases, allow one to avoid its explicit evaluation through the definition above.

=== Convergent series ===
[[Image:Exponential integral.svg|300px|right|thumb| Plot of {{math|''E''{{sub|1}}}} function (top) and {{math|Ei}} function (bottom).]]

For real or complex arguments off the negative real axis, <math>E_1(z)</math> can be expressed as{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=229|loc=5.1.11}}
<math display="block">E_1(z) = -\gamma - \ln z - \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-z)^k}{k\; k!} \qquad (\left| \operatorname{Arg}(z) \right| < \pi)</math>
where <math>\gamma</math> is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]]. The sum converges for all complex {{tmath|z}}, and we take the usual value of the [[complex logarithm]] having a [[branch cut]] along the negative real axis.

This formula can be used to compute <math>E_1(x)</math> with floating point operations for real <math>x</math> between {{tmath|0}} and {{tmath|2.5}}. For {{tmath|x > 2.5}}, the result is inaccurate due to [[Catastrophic cancellation|cancellation]].

A faster converging series was found by [[Ramanujan]]:{{sfn|ps=|Andrews|Berndt|2013|p=130|loc=24.16}}
<math display="block">\mathrm{Ei} (x) = \gamma + \ln x + \exp{(x/2)} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{ (-1)^{n-1} x^n} {n! \, 2^{n-1}} \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor} \frac{1}{2k+1}</math>

=== Asymptotic (divergent) series ===
[[Image:AsymptoticExpansionE1.png|right|400px|thumb| Relative error of the asymptotic approximation for different number {{mvar|N}} of terms in the truncated sum]]

The convergence of the series above is slow for arguments of larger modulus. For example, more than 40 terms are required to get an answer correct to three [[significant figures]] for {{tmath|E_1(10)}}.{{sfn|ps=|Bleistein|Handelsman|1986|p=2}} However, for positive values of {{tmath|x}}, there is a [[divergent series]] approximation that can be obtained by integrating <math>x e^x E_1(x)</math> by parts:{{sfn|ps=|Bleistein|Handelsman|1986|p=3}}
<math display="block">E_1(x)=\frac{\exp(-x)} x \left(\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \frac{n!}{(-x)^n} +O(N!x^{-N}) \right)</math>
The relative error of the approximation above is plotted on the figure to the right for various values of {{tmath|N}}, the number of terms in the truncated sum ({{tmath|1= N=1 }} in red, <math>N=5</math> in pink).

==== Asymptotics beyond all orders ====
[[File:Normalized exponential integral.png|400px|thumb|Normalized exponential integral. The value plotted is {{math| {{sfrac|Ei(''x'')|(exp ''x'')/''x''|font-size= 0.75em;}}}}. The values of {{mvar|x}} are written above the corresponding point. The horizontal spacing is according to {{math|arctan ''x''}}. The graph is extended "beyond infinity" a little on both the right and the left to show how the normalized function behaves when {{math| 1/''x''}} is small. (The horizontal spacing for these points corresponds to angles whose tangent is {{mvar|x}}.)]]

Using [[integration by parts]], we can obtain an explicit formula<ref>{{cite book |last= O’Malley |first= Robert E. |chapter= Asymptotic Approximations |date= 2014 |title= Historical Developments in Singular Perturbations |pages=27–51 |editor-last= O'Malley |editor-first= Robert E. |place= Cham |publisher= Springer International Publishing |language= en |doi= 10.1007/978-3-319-11924-3_2 |isbn= 978-3-319-11924-3 }}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{Ei}(z) &= \frac{e^{z}} {z} \left (\sum _{k=0}^{n} \frac{k!} {z^{k}} + e_{n}(z)\right), \\
e_{n}(z) &\equiv (n + 1)!\ ze^{-z}\int _{ -\infty }^{z} \frac{e^{t}} {t^{n+2}}\,dt.
\end{align}</math>
For any fixed {{tmath|z}}, the absolute value of the error term <math>|e_n(z)|</math> decreases, then increases. The minimum occurs at {{tmath| n\sim \vert z\vert }}, at which point {{tmath|\textstyle \vert e_{n}(z)\vert \leq \sqrt{\frac{2\pi } {\vert z\vert } }e^{-\vert z\vert } }}. This bound is said to be "asymptotics beyond all orders".

=== Exponential and logarithmic behavior: bracketing ===
[[Image:BracketingE1.png|right|200px|thumb|Bracketing of {{math|''E''{{sub|1}}}} by elementary functions]]

From the two series suggested in previous subsections, it follows that <math>E_1</math> behaves like a negative exponential for large values of the argument and like a logarithm for small values. For positive real values of the argument, <math>E_1</math> can be bracketed by elementary functions as follows:{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=229|loc=5.1.20}}
<math display="block">
\frac 1 2 e^{-x}\,\ln\!\left( 1+\frac 2 x \right)
< E_1(x) < e^{-x}\,\ln\!\left( 1+\frac 1 x \right)
\qquad x>0
</math>

The left-hand side of this inequality is shown in the graph to the left in blue; the central part <math>E_1(x)</math> is shown in black and the right-hand side is shown in red.

=== Definition by Ein ===

Both <math>\operatorname{Ei}</math> and <math>E_1</math> can be written more simply using the [[entire function]] {{tmath|\operatorname{Ein} }}{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=228|loc=see footnote 3}} defined as
<math display="block">
\operatorname{Ein}(z)
= \int_0^z (1-e^{-t})\frac{dt}{t}
= \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{k+1}z^k}{k\; k!}
</math>
(note that this is just the [[alternating series]] in the above definition of {{tmath|E_1}}). Then we have
<math display="block">\begin{align}
E_1(z) &= -\gamma - \ln z + \operatorname{Ein}(z), && \left| \operatorname{Arg}(z) \right| < \pi; \\
\operatorname{Ei}(x) &= \hphantom{-}\gamma + \ln{x} - \mathrm{Ein}(-x), && x \neq 0.
\end{align}</math>
The function <math>\operatorname{Ein}</math> is related to the exponential [[generating function]] of the [[harmonic numbers]]:
<math display="block">
\operatorname{Ein}(z) = e^{-z} \, \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac {z^n}{n!} H_n
</math>

=== Relation with other functions ===
Kummer's equation
<math display="block">z\frac{d^2w}{dz^2} + (b-z)\frac{dw}{dz} - aw = 0</math>
is usually solved by the [[confluent hypergeometric functions]] <math>M(a,b,z)</math> and {{tmath|U(a,b,z)}}. But when <math>a=0</math> and {{tmath|1= b=1}}, that is,
<math display="block">z\frac{d^2w}{dz^2} + (1-z)\frac{dw}{dz} = 0</math>
we have
<math display="block">M(0,1,z)=U(0,1,z)=1</math>
for all {{tmath|z}}. A second solution is then given by {{tmath|E_1(-z)}}. In fact,
<math display="block">E_1(-z)=-\gamma-i\pi+\frac{\partial[U(a,1,z)-M(a,1,z)]}{\partial a},\qquad 0< \operatorname{Arg}(z)<2\pi</math>
with the derivative evaluated at {{tmath|1= a=0 }}. Another connexion with the confluent hypergeometric functions is that {{tmath|E_1}} is an exponential times the function {{tmath|U(1,1,z)}}:
<math display="block">E_1(z)=e^{-z}U(1,1,z)</math>

The exponential integral is closely related to the [[logarithmic integral function]] {{tmath| \operatorname{li}(e^x) }} by the formula
<math display="block">\operatorname{li}(e^x) = \operatorname{Ei}(x)</math>
for non-zero real values of {{tmath|x}}.

The series expansion of the exponential integral immediately gives rise to an expression in terms of the generalized hypergeometric function {{tmath|{}_2\!F_2}}:
<math display="block">\operatorname{Ei}(x) = x{\,}_2\!F_2(1,1;2,2;x)+\ln x+\gamma.</math>

=== Generalization ===
The exponential integral may also be generalized to
<math display="block">E_n(x) = \int_1^\infty \frac{e^{-xt}}{t^n}\, dt,</math>
which can be written as a special case of the upper [[incomplete gamma function]]:{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=230|loc=5.1.45}}
<math display="block">E_n(x) =x^{n-1}\Gamma(1-n,x).</math>

The generalized form is sometimes called the Misra function {{tmath|\varphi_m(x)}},{{efn|After R. D. Misra; {{harvnb|Misra|Born|1940|p=178}}.}}{{efn|Many properties of this generalized form can be found in {{harvnb|DLMF 8.19}}.}} defined as
<math display="block">\varphi_m(x)=E_{-m}(x).</math>

Including a logarithm defines the generalized integro-exponential function{{sfn|Milgram|1985}}
<math display="block">E_s^j(z)= \frac{1}{\Gamma(j+1)}\int_1^\infty \left(\log t\right)^j \frac{e^{-zt}}{t^s}\,dt.</math>

=== Derivatives ===

The derivatives of the generalised functions <math>E_n</math> can be calculated by means of the formula{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=230|loc=5.1.26}}
<math display="block">
E_n '(z) = - E_{n-1}(z) \qquad (n=1,2,3,\ldots)
</math>
Note that the function <math>E_0</math> is easy to evaluate (making this recursion useful), since it is just {{tmath|\textstyle \frac{e^{-z} }{z} }}.{{sfn|ps=|Abramowitz|Stegun|1964|p=229|loc=5.1.24}}

=== Exponential integral of imaginary argument ===

[[Image:E1ofImaginaryArgument.png|right|200px|thumb|{{math|''E''{{sub|1}}(''ix'')}}
against {{mvar|x}}; real part black, imaginary part red.]]

If <math>z</math> is imaginary, it has a nonnegative real part, so we can use the formula
<math display="block">
E_1(z) = \int_1^\infty
\frac{e^{-tz}} t \, dt
</math>
to get a relation with the [[trigonometric integral]]s <math>\operatorname{Si}</math> and {{tmath|\operatorname{Ci} }}:
<math display="block">
E_1(ix) = i\left[ -\tfrac{1}{2}\pi + \operatorname{Si}(x)\right] - \operatorname{Ci}(x)
\qquad (x > 0)
</math>
The real and imaginary parts of <math>E_1(ix)</math> are plotted in the figure to the right with black and red curves.

=== Approximations ===
There have been a number of approximations for the exponential integral function. These include:

* The Swamee and Ohija approximation<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |title = Revisit of Well Function Approximation and An Easy Graphical Curve Matching Technique for Theis' Solution |journal = Ground Water|date = 2003-05-01 |issn = 1745-6584 |pages = 387–390 |volume = 41 | issue = 3 |doi = 10.1111/j.1745-6584.2003.tb02608.x |first = Pham Huy |last = Giao |pmid=12772832 |bibcode=2003GrWat..41..387G |s2cid=31982931 }}</ref> <math display="block">E_1(x) = \left (A^{-7.7}+B \right )^{-0.13},</math> where <math display="block">\begin{align}
A &= \ln\left [\left (\frac{0.56146}{x}+0.65\right)(1+x)\right] \\
B &= x^4e^{7.7x}(2+x)^{3.7}
\end{align}</math>       
* The Allen and Hastings approximation<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{cite journal |title = Numerical evaluation of exponential integral: Theis well function approximation |journal = Journal of Hydrology |date = 1998-02-26 |pages = 38–51 |volume = 205 |issue = 1–2 |doi = 10.1016/S0022-1694(97)00134-0 |first1 = Peng-Hsiang |last1 = Tseng |first2 = Tien-Chang |last2 = Lee |bibcode = 1998JHyd..205...38T }}</ref> <math display="block">E_1(x) = \begin{cases} - \ln x +\textbf{a}^\mathsf{T}\textbf{x}_5,&x\leq1 \\ \frac{e^{-x}} x \frac{\textbf{b}^\mathsf{T} \textbf{x}_3}{\textbf{c}^\mathsf{T}\textbf{x}_3},&x\geq1 \end{cases}</math> where <math display="block">\begin{align}
\textbf{a} & \triangleq [-0.57722, 0.99999, -0.24991, 0.05519, -0.00976, 0.00108]^\mathsf{T} \\
\textbf{b} & \triangleq[0.26777,8.63476, 18.05902, 8.57333]^\mathsf{T} \\
\textbf{c} & \triangleq[3.95850, 21.09965, 25.63296, 9.57332]^\mathsf{T} \\
\textbf{x}_k &\triangleq[x^0,x^1,\dots, x^k]^\mathsf{T}
\end{align}</math>
* The [[continued fraction]] expansion<ref name=":1" /> <math display="block">E_1(x) = \cfrac{e^{-x}}{x+\cfrac{1}{1+\cfrac{1}{x+\cfrac{2}{1+\cfrac{2}{x+\cfrac{3}{\ddots}}}}}}.</math>
* The approximation of Barry ''et al.''<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Approximation for the exponential integral (Theis well function) |journal = Journal of Hydrology|date = 2000-01-31| pages = 287–291|volume = 227|issue = 1–4|doi = 10.1016/S0022-1694(99)00184-5|first1 = D. A|last1 = Barry|first2 = J. -Y|last2 = Parlange |first3 = L|last3 = Li|bibcode = 2000JHyd..227..287B }}</ref> <math display="block">E_1(x) = \frac{e^{-x}}{G+(1-G)e^{-\frac{x}{1-G}}}\ln\left[1+\frac G x -\frac{1-G}{(h+bx)^2}\right],</math> where: <math display="block">\begin{align}
h &= \frac{1}{1+x\sqrt{x}}+\frac{h_{\infty}q}{1+q} \\
q &=\frac{20}{47}x^{\sqrt{\frac{31}{26}}} \\
h_{\infty} &= \frac{(1-G)(G^2-6G+12)}{3G(2-G)^2b} \\
b &=\sqrt{\frac{2(1-G)}{G(2-G)}} \\
G &= e^{-\gamma}
\end{align}</math> with <math>\gamma</math> being the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]].

== Inverse function of the exponential integral ==
{{User-generated|section|date=June 2026}}
We can express the [[Inverse function]] of the exponential integral in [[power series]] form:<ref>{{cite web |title=Inverse function of the exponential integral {{math|Ei{{sup|−1}}(''x'')}} |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4901881/inverse-function-of-the-exponential-integral-mathrmei-1x |access-date=2024-04-24 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=}}</ref>
<math display="block">\forall |x| < \frac{\mu}{\ln(\mu)},\quad \operatorname{Ei}^{-1}(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} \frac{P_n(\ln(\mu))}{\mu^n}</math>
where <math>\mu</math> is the [[Ramanujan–Soldner constant]] and <math>(P_n)</math> is [[polynomial]] sequence defined by the following [[recurrence relation]]:
<math display="block">P_0(x) = x,\ P_{n+1}(x) = x(P_n'(x) - nP_n(x)).</math>

For {{tmath| n > 0 }}, <math>\deg P_n = n</math> and we have the formula:
<math display="block">P_n(x) = \left.\left(\frac{d}{dt}\right)^{n-1} \left(\frac{te^x}{\operatorname{Ei}(t+x)-\operatorname{Ei}(x)}\right)^n\right|_{t=0}.</math>

== Applications ==
* Time-dependent [[heat transfer]]
* Nonequilibrium [[groundwater]] flow in the [[Aquifer test#Transient Theis solution|Theis solution]] (called a ''well function'')
* Radiative transfer in stellar and planetary atmospheres
* Radial diffusivity equation for transient or unsteady state flow with line sources and sinks
* Solutions to the [[neutron transport]] equation in simplified 1-D geometries<ref>{{cite book |title=Nuclear Reactor Theory |year=1970 |publisher=Van Nostrand Reinhold Company|author=George I. Bell |author2=Samuel Glasstone }}</ref>
* Solutions to the [[Trachenko–Zaccone]] [[List of nonlinear ordinary differential equations|nonlinear differential equation]] for the [[stretched exponential function]] in the relaxation of [[amorphous solids]] and [[glass transition]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Trachenko |first1=K. |last2=Zaccone |first2=A.|date=2021-06-14 |title=Slow stretched-exponential and fast compressed-exponential relaxation from local event dynamics |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-648X/ac04cd |journal=Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter |language=en |volume=33 |issue= 31|pages=315101 |doi= 10.1088/1361-648X/ac04cd|pmid=34034250 |bibcode= 2021JPCM...33E5101T|issn=0953-8984|arxiv=2010.10440 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ginzburg |first1=V. V. |last2=Gendelman | first2= O. V. |last3=Zaccone |first3=A.|date=2024-02-23 |title=Unifying Physical Framework for Stretched-Exponential, Compressed-Exponential, and Logarithmic Relaxation Phenomena in Glassy Polymers|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.macromol.3c02480 |journal=Macromolecules |language=en |volume=57 |issue= 5|pages=2520–2529 |doi= 10.1021/acs.macromol.3c02480|bibcode= 2024MaMol..57.2520G|issn=0024-9297 |arxiv=2311.09321 }}</ref>
